title: Do Orthogonality Constraints Help Language-Model Training Beyond Sphere Optimization?

paper.title: Do Orthogonality Constraints Help Language-Model Training Beyond Sphere Optimization?
paper.abstract:
Abstract A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in
fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open
question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We
conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with
models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens.
We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the
weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it.
Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of
freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every d d rows form a
row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size d d is a hyperparameter. Among
block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no d > 1 d>1 used
throughout the network reliably outperforms d = 1 d=1 , and large blocks are clearly
worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the
query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 , the
constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own
unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a
diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream
accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the
realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model
pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with
several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning
that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is
attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization,
or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Before the rise of large language models (LLMs), weight orthogonality was used to keep networks with millions of parameters well conditioned and their feature directions nonredundant ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) . For modern pretrained models, orthogonal fine-tuning methods report gains from learning orthogonal transformations of pretrained weights ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) or from constraining low-rank adapter factors to Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2025 ) . In LLM pre-training, orthogonality has so far mostly shaped the training dynamics rather than the weights: the Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the update to each weight matrix, and POET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random weight matrix, preserving its singular values. Research blogs ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) derive optimizers that keep the weights themselves on the Stiefel manifold, without large-scale language-model experiments. Yoshihara (2026) evaluates this approach in GPT-2 models with up to 124M parameters and assigns different orthogonality structures to attention and MLP matrices. Whether keeping the weights themselves orthogonal helps LLM pre-training at scale remains open. We study this question systematically with decoder-only models from 360M to 3.1B parameters trained on nearly 200B tokens. The most direct form of orthogonality training requires an entire weight matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m ≤ n m\leq n to have orthonormal rows, W ​ W ⊤ = I m WW^{\top}=I_{m} . This is a very strong regularization. It imposes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 constraints in total, so a square orthonormal matrix loses about half of its degrees of freedom, i.e., the number of effective parameters is roughly halved. We explored two routes for recovering the lost degrees of freedom. The first route relaxes the orthogonality constraint on W W to an orthogonal reparameterization of W W . The simplest variant adds per-row magnitudes: the model learns a row-orthonormal factor Q Q and a positive diagonal factor D D , and the effective weight is W = D ​ Q W=DQ . This reparameterization can represent every matrix whose rows are orthogonal and nonzero, but it recovers only m m degrees of freedom. Even with these magnitudes, full-matrix orthogonality substantially worsens validation loss, whether it is enforced by our projected update or by manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ) (Figure 1 ; Appendix M ). To go one step further, recall that every full-rank matrix admits a polar decomposition; we therefore replace the diagonal factor D D with a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix S S , so that W = S ​ Q W=SQ . This reparameterization recovers all m ​ n mn degrees of freedom: S S contributes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 and Q Q contributes m ​ n − m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 mn-m(m+1)/2 . A triangular factor ( W = T ​ Q W=TQ ) and a singular-value form ( W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} ) are equally expressive, but in training they recover much less of the constraint penalty than SPD, and the singular-value form recovers almost none. The second route relaxes the constraint itself. An n × n n\times n square matrix is partitioned into n / d n/d blocks of size d × n d\times n , and only each block is required to have orthonormal rows, so the number of constraints falls to n ⁡ ( d + 1 ) / 2 n(d+1)/2 . The block size d d becomes a single knob that ranges from d = 1 d=1 , which constrains only the row norms, to the shorter side of the matrix. Increasing d d adds exactly one thing: zero inner products between rows in the same block. The two routes combine: each block is reparameterized with per-row magnitudes, W k = D k ​ Q k W_{k}=D_{k}Q_{k} , or with an SPD factor, W k = S k ​ Q k W_{k}=S_{k}Q_{k} . Our main comparison uses per-row magnitudes at every block size, so increasing d d changes only the orthogonality between rows. In the special case d = 1 d=1 , the SPD factor reduces to the per-row magnitude, and the constraint reduces to a sphere constraint on each row with a learnable magnitude. Combining several ways to train orthonormal matrices with several ways to recover the lost degrees of freedom, we test fourteen variants, together with three alternative updates for the sphere control (Table 10 ), in pre-training Llama-style LLMs of three sizes, 360M, 1.3B, and 3.1B parameters, with token budgets from 2 × 2\times to 16 × 16\times the Chinchilla-optimal budget. No block size d > 1 d>1 used throughout the network reliably improves on d = 1 d=1 . Small blocks are indistinguishable from d = 1 d=1 , and the penalty grows steadily with block size. SPD factors, which restore mixing between rows of a block, recover much of this penalty at moderate block sizes but give no consistent advantage, and the other realizations trail d = 1 d=1 as well. The one placement that helps, SPD factors on the query and key projections, gives a small gain in our smallest model that fades as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 the orthogonality constraint reduces to sphere optimization: each row direction lives on its own unit sphere with a learned magnitude, and no relation between rows is imposed. We thus arrive, from the orthogonality side, at the direction–magnitude geometry of recent row-norm methods ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ; Hägele et al., 2026 ) , and like them we find that it improves on tuned Muon, as well as on MuonH, which fixes the Frobenius norm of each matrix ( Wen et al., 2026a ) , at every scale we trained. Across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows adds nothing beyond sphere optimization. However, the implementation of sphere optimization also matters: weight normalization ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) trained with Muon has the same expressiveness but recovers less than half of the improvement over Muon. This conclusion appears to conflict with several reports of orthogonality gains, so we re-examine five of them in pre-training and fine-tuning. The released implementations of POET and Pion store the AdamW baseline in bfloat16; with fp32 storage, AdamW improves by 80 to 150 milli-loss, POET’s short-run advantage shrinks from 31 to 9 milli-loss and reverses with longer training, and Pion trails AdamW by 95 milli-loss at 1.3B. For module-wise constraints, projected diagonal-Gram training trails a reparameterization that targets the same row geometry, and neither diagonal-Gram nor Stiefel blocks improve on d = 1 d=1 in the module to which they are assigned. In StelLA, replacing Euclidean adapter factors with sphere-constrained ones gains 2.1 accuracy points, and adding Stiefel constraints on top changes accuracy by − 0.09 -0.09 . In PSOFT, replacing the orthogonal latent transformation with independently normalized rows does not reduce accuracy. In each case, the reported gain traces to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to orthogonality between rows. Our contributions are: • A block-wise orthogonality family whose block size moves from sphere optimization to the largest Stiefel blocks each matrix allows while holding row magnitudes fixed, so that its effect isolates orthogonality between rows. • A pre-training study from 360M to 3.1B parameters showing that no block size above one used throughout the network improves on sphere optimization, that SPD factors on query and key projections give a small gain that vanishes as models grow, and that sphere optimization itself improves on tuned Muon; the same holds for a diffusion transformer on ImageNet, and fine-tuned models show no downstream advantage for any block size. • Re-examinations of five orthogonality methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that trace each reported gain to a factor other than orthogonality between rows.

sections.heading: Orthogonality in neural-network training.
sections.text: Orthogonal weights have been pursued through tight-frame, reparameterization, penalty, and manifold methods ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ; Bansal et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , distinct from spectral normalization ( Miyato et al., 2018 ) ; classical treatments develop the underlying matrix-manifold algorithms ( Edelman et al., 1998 ; Absil et al., 2008 ) . In the RNN study of Vorontsov et al. (2017) , soft orthogonality outperformed exact constraints. We compare hard block constraints with a norm-matched sphere control; soft orthogonality penalties are not evaluated here.

sections.heading: Geometry in parameter-efficient adaptation.
sections.text: Orthogonality can constrain transformations of pretrained weights, SVD-like or initialized LoRA factors, or manifold-optimized adapters ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Büyükakyüz, 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Bogachev et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These constructions act on different objects. Our adaptation study compares sphere and Stiefel constraints within StelLA’s two-factor U ​ S ​ V ⊤ USV^{\top} parameterization.

sections.heading: Geometry-aware language-model pretraining.
sections.text: Muon orthogonalizes matrix-valued updates, while manifold Muon asks how to optimize a Stiefel-constrained weight ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2026b ; Su, 2025 ; Bernstein, 2025 ; Solonko et al., 2026 ) ; we ask whether that constraint improves over a sphere control with matched gains. Related methods control Frobenius or operator norms, normalize update directions, or impose module-wise Stiefel and DGram geometry ( Wen et al., 2026a ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Gu and Xie, 2026 ; Yoshihara, 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . POET and Pion use orthogonal transformations but do not require orthogonal effective-weight rows ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Normalization and magnitude–direction separation.
sections.text: Weight normalization separates direction from magnitude ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) . Muown is the closest prior parameterization to our d = 1 d=1 control ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ) ; related work studies row or column gains, broader parameter normalization, and magnitude–direction decompositions in adaptation ( Hägele et al., 2026 ; Velikanov et al., 2026 ; Loshchilov et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . Our d = 1 d=1 control confirms this norm-and-scale line; the new comparison begins when d d increases while per-row gains remain fixed. Concurrent work traces the gains of fixed-norm training largely to its effective learning rate ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Appendix A gives an extended discussion.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We build every constrained variant on Muon. Section 3.1 describes a general recipe for training a matrix with orthonormal rows, and Section 3.2 applies it to row blocks of Transformer weights and describes how we return the degrees of freedom that the constraint removes. Appendix D describes the other optimizers and controls we compare.

sections.heading: 3.2 Recovering degrees of freedom
sections.text: Let W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a matrix-shaped Transformer weight. We partition its rows into m / d m/d contiguous blocks and keep the directional factor of each block, Q k Q_{k} , on St ⁡ ( d , n ) \operatorname{St}(d,n) . The Muon direction and scale are computed for the whole matrix; each block is then projected and retracted independently as in Section 3.1 . When m ≤ n m\leq n , d = m d=m constrains the whole matrix.

sections.heading: Reparameterization.
sections.text: The first route forms each effective block from its orthonormal factor and a magnitude factor. With per-row magnitudes, W k = D k ​ Q k , D k = diag ⁡ ( a k ) , W k ​ W k ⊤ = D k 2 , W_{k}=D_{k}Q_{k},\qquad D_{k}=\operatorname{diag}(a_{k}),\qquad W_{k}W_{k}^{\top}=D_{k}^{2}, (4) so the effective rows stay orthogonal while each keeps its own learned norm. To allow mixing between rows, we replace D k D_{k} with an SPD factor, W k = S k ​ Q k , S k = L k ​ L k ⊤ , L k = diag ⁡ ( a k ) + tril ⁡ ( M k , − 1 ) . W_{k}=S_{k}Q_{k},\qquad S_{k}=L_{k}L_{k}^{\top},\qquad L_{k}=\operatorname{diag}(a_{k})+\operatorname{tril}(M_{k},-1). (5) Now W k ​ W k ⊤ = S k 2 W_{k}W_{k}^{\top}=S_{k}^{2} is generally dense, so the effective rows are no longer orthogonal, and by the polar decomposition this form can represent any full-row-rank block. We initialize S k = I d S_{k}=I_{d} . The magnitude factors a k a_{k} and L k L_{k} are trained with AdamW. Other left factors, including triangular ( W k = T k ​ Q k W_{k}=T_{k}Q_{k} ), singular-value ( W k = U k ​ Σ k ​ Q k W_{k}=U_{k}\Sigma_{k}Q_{k} with U k U_{k} orthogonal), and other symmetric forms, are equally expressive and are defined in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Block size.
sections.text: The second route shrinks the set of constrained row pairs. With per-row magnitudes at every d d , an m m -row matrix has m ⁡ ( d − 1 ) / 2 m(d-1)/2 row pairs constrained to be orthogonal, a fraction ( d − 1 ) / ( m − 1 ) (d-1)/(m-1) of all pairs, while the number of row norms and the way they are optimized stay the same. Increasing d d therefore changes only the orthogonality between rows. At d = 1 d=1 , the directions form a product of unit spheres (the oblique manifold ( Absil and Gallivan, 2006 ) ), the SPD factor reduces to the per-row magnitude, and the model has the same function class as an unconstrained row with no constraint between rows. We call this case sphere optimization.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental design and tuning
sections.text: We train decoder-only Transformers with 360M, 1.3B, and 3.1B parameters at context length 4096. Muon-family runs scale decoupled weight decay by the Muon learning rate ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and use cosine decay to 0.01 0.01 times the peak learning rate. Tuned Muon, which shapes the update spectrum without constraining the trained weight to be orthogonal, serves as our principal unconstrained baseline. Our primary corpus is C4 ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) . Budgets are reported as multiples of 20 tokens per parameter, the representative Chinchilla ratio ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Unless stated otherwise, we report final target-step cross-entropy on C4-val, a fixed evaluation set drawn from the C4 validation split. Muon, MuonH, and the d = 1 d=1 control receive separate main-learning-rate sweeps; unconstrained baselines also tune weight decay. The AdamW-side learning rate is fixed at 0.0012 across the Muon-family arms. For the 360M d d -ladder, a bracket over { 0.001 , 0.002 , 0.004 } \{0.001,0.002,0.004\} selects the common interior value 0.002 0.002 for each d d , including d = 32 d=32 . Main-text entries are means over seeds; each seed sets the initialization and, except at 1.3B, 7.77 × 7.77\times , the order of the training data; Appendix F gives seed counts, per-seed losses, and paired intervals, and Appendices B – S give additional grids. We report loss differences in milli-loss ( 10 − 3 10^{-3} nats), each measured against a matched d = 1 d=1 run (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Block orthogonality provides no measured gain
sections.text: The headline comparison holds norm treatment and gain granularity fixed. Every d = 1 , 8 , 32 d=1,8,32 model retains one learned gain per row; increasing d d makes rows within each block orthogonal to each other. At 2 × 2\times , 4 × 4\times , and 7.69 × 7.69\times , d = 8 d=8 changes mean loss by only 0.8–1.1 milli-loss, whereas d = 32 d=32 increases it by 3.7–5.2 milli-loss (Table 1 ; Appendix G for 4 × 4\times ). Because per-row blocks with d > 1 d>1 also remove directions within each block, this ladder measures the constraint together with its cost in expressivity; the matrix-gain controls of Section 4.3 restore that expressivity and isolate the geometry. Every block size also uses unit-norm rows and the same gains, so the effective learning rate of the directions, which recent work identifies as a main driver of fixed-norm training ( van Laarhoven, 2017 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , is the same across the ladder. Training to 16 × 16\times narrows the d = 32 d=32 gap to 2.4 milli-loss, which still corresponds to about 5% more training steps (Appendix H ). sections.heading: 4.3 Expressivity and optimizer controls for d > 1 d>1
sections.text: We tested diagonal and matrix-valued gains together with projected diagonal-Gram (DGram) training, which keeps W ​ W ⊤ WW^{\top} diagonal by projection while leaving row norms free. SPD uses S = L ​ L ⊤ S=LL^{\top} , XXT uses S = X ​ X ⊤ S=XX^{\top} , and XXT+diagonal uses S = diag ⁡ ( a ) + X ​ X ⊤ S=\operatorname{diag}(a)+XX^{\top} . At 360M, SPD and XXT close the 6.5 milli-loss deficit of one scalar gain per block, to within 0.3 milli-loss of d = 1 d=1 (Table 2 ), consistent with restoring within-block degrees of freedom, including row mixing. Trained d = 1 d=1 rows are about as decorrelated as random directions: within 32-row windows, their mean absolute cosine is 0.030 (0.047 in query and key matrices), against 0.025 for random directions in ℝ 1024 \mathbb{R}^{1024} and 0.032 and 0.034 for tuned Muon and MuonH. Per-row d = 32 d=32 sets the within-block value to zero, and the SPD gain raises it to 0.052 (Appendix N ). Expressivity alone does not decide this: equally expressive triangular and singular-value factors recover much less (Table 28 ). Larger blocks widen the gap (Figure 1 ): at d ≥ 128 d\geq 128 , every tested per-row and SPD configuration trails d = 1 d=1 at both 360M and 1.3B, by more at each larger d d . Matrix-valued gains, which allow nonorthogonal effective rows, show no consistent advantage over d = 1 d=1 when every matrix uses them. At d = 32 d=32 , SPD differs from d = 1 d=1 by − 0.2 -0.2 milli-loss at 360M, − 1.0 -1.0 at 1.3B, and − 0.3 -0.3 at 3.1B, and by − 0.4 -0.4 and − 0.7 -0.7 on the FPO mixture at 2 × 2\times and 4 × 4\times . These comparisons train every gain at the shared default learning rate. Raising the gain learning rate of d = 1 d=1 to 0.0048 makes SPD 0.6 milli-loss worse than d = 1 d=1 at 1.3B, whereas SPD’s own factor learning rate is already best at the default (Appendix R ). At 1.3B, d = 64 d=64 SPD trails d = 1 d=1 by 1.0 milli-loss. Manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) solves the constrained spectral-norm steepest-descent problem directly but trails d = 1 d=1 at every tested block size, budget, and scale: by 26–142 milli-loss at 360M and by 23–63 milli-loss at 1.3B (Appendix M ). It improves on projected OrthMuon only at the largest tested block size at 360M and trails it at every tested block size at 1.3B, so the negative result is not specific to the projected update.

sections.heading: 4.4 Row mixing in queries and keys helps only small models
sections.text: One placement of SPD factors does improve on d = 1 d=1 , but the gain fades as models grow. We give the query and key projections SPD factors with block size 64 and keep every other matrix at d = 1 d=1 . The reference is d = 1 d=1 throughout with its gain learning rate raised to 0.0048, which improves on the default by 0.6–1.8 milli-loss at 360M, 1.5 at 1.3B, and 0.3 at 3.1B (Appendix R ). Against this reference, SPD factors on queries and keys lower the loss by 4.6 milli-loss at 360M, 2 × 2\times . Queries and keys contribute about equally, whereas SPD factors on value, output, or MLP projections do not help (Table 3 ). The gain shrinks with training length, to 3.3 milli-loss at 4 × 4\times and 2.7 at 7.69 × 7.69\times , and with model size, to 1.1 at 1.3B and 0.7 at 3.1B (Appendix Q ). Larger blocks reverse the effect. At 3.1B, whose heads have 128 rows, d = 128 d=128 SPD factors on queries and keys are 0.7 milli-loss worse than the reference. sections.heading: 4.5 The d = 1 d=1 control is strong but optimizer-dependent
sections.text: The d = 1 d=1 control improves over tuned Muon at the shared AdamW-side learning rate (Section 4 ), confirming the positive norm-and-scale results reported by recent work ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ; Hägele et al., 2026 ) . Across three budgets, it lowers validation loss by 13.1–17.7 milli-loss; the unit-row constraint without gain and the learned row magnitudes each contribute about half (Table 4 ). MuonH, which controls one Frobenius norm per matrix, is within 0.6 milli-loss of the no-gain d = 1 d=1 model at 2 × 2\times and 4 × 4\times and 2.7 milli-loss better at 7.69 × 7.69\times . Its deficit to d = 1 d=1 lies mainly in attention: 7.5 milli-loss there versus 1.4 in MLP matrices (Appendix P ). Applying Muon to an unconstrained latent weight and normalizing rows only in the forward pass reaches 2.4697. It recovers 5.5 of the 13.1 milli-loss improvement over Muon and remains 7.6 milli-loss behind explicit sphere-coordinate optimization. The coordinate system and update dynamics therefore matter alongside norm and scale. Concurrent work attributes most of the advantage of fixed-norm training over weight decay to its effective-learning-rate trajectory ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) ; part of the gain of d = 1 d=1 over Muon may arise the same way, whereas the learned row gains, which supply about half of it, are part of the parameterization. Alternative gain coordinates, direct row normalization, and tangent or transported momentum remain within 1.6 milli-loss of the explicit d = 1 d=1 result (Appendix S ).

sections.heading: 4.6 Scope across scale, data, modality, and fine-tuning
sections.text: Changing the training mixture preserves the matched diagonal-gain ordering. With the FPO-mix training mixture—92.57% DCLM, 6.09% StarCoder, and 1.34% ProofPile ( Wen et al., 2026b ) —and C4-val evaluation, d = 1 d=1 again leads MuonH and Muon at 360M and 1.3B, and per-row-gain d = 32 d=32 at 360M (Table 1 ; Appendix K ). On held-out web text, C4-trained 360M checkpoints keep the C4 ordering at about its C4 magnitude: on the FPO mixture and DCLM, per-row d = 8 d=8 and d = 32 d=32 match d = 1 d=1 , Muon and MuonH trail it by 7 to 14 milli-loss, and AdamW by about 90. On StarCoder, ProofPile, and OLM-arXiv, loss varies by 60–100 milli-loss between training runs of the same configuration, and no ordering among block sizes or baselines emerges (Appendix L ). The strength of the d = 1 d=1 control also extends beyond 360M. At 1.3B, it improves over Muon by 12.8, 13.1, and 12.0 milli-loss at 2 × 2\times , 4 × 4\times , and 7.77 × 7.77\times , and by 12.0 at 3.1B; Appendix J reports the full scaling table. The per-row d = 32 d=32 penalty shrinks with scale (Table 2 ), as does the query–key SPD gain, so both effects of row structure approach zero in the tested range; at 360M the d = 32 d=32 penalty corresponds to about 5% more training steps at every budget up to 16 × 16\times (Appendix H ). Sphere optimization also improves image generation. In a 130M-parameter diffusion transformer (SiT-B/2) trained on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 with query–key normalization, d = 1 d=1 lowers FID-50K from 25.50 to 24.60 with an Adam inner optimizer and from 21.55 to 20.81 with Muon, and lowers validation loss in both families. Query and key blocks of 64 rows do not improve on d = 1 d=1 , and an SPD factor on those blocks ties it (Appendix T ). Without query–key normalization, AdamW and d = 1 d=1 occasionally diverge late in training, whereas scalar-gain d > 1 d>1 blocks, which bound the query–key product, never do. Query–key normalization removes these divergences and gives lower FID than d > 1 d>1 without it, so the stability benefit of d > 1 d>1 traces to logit control rather than to orthogonality between rows. Fine-tuning does not separate the parameterizations either. After full fine-tuning of the 3.1B models on Commonsense170K, with the merged weights trained by one AdamW recipe, eight-task accuracy differs from the matched d = 1 d=1 model by at most 0.4 points for every d > 1 d>1 and query–key configuration, well within the variation between fine-tuning runs. Muon and MuonH trail d = 1 d=1 by 0.7 and 1.1 points. Fine-tuning the merged weights with AdamW raises every model by 1.5 to 3.1 points over continuing with its pretraining optimizer (Appendix U ).

sections.heading: POET and Pion: precision and training horizon.
sections.text: POET learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random base matrix and preserves its initialized singular-value spectrum ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) . Pion, from the same group, turns this construction into an optimizer that updates each weight through left and right orthogonal transformations ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Both released implementations store the AdamW baseline’s parameters and optimizer moments in bfloat16, and in both cases fp32 storage makes AdamW far stronger (Table 6 ). In POET’s harness at 197M tokens, with independently swept learning rates, bfloat16 raises AdamW loss by 149 milli-loss and POET loss by 127, because POET’s factors start at zero or identity and its moments are periodically reset. POET’s advantage shrinks from 31.2 to 8.7 milli-loss, and it does not survive longer training: in a separate 130M implementation, POET leads tuned AdamW by 370 and 61 milli-loss at 0.59B and 2B tokens but trails by 8 and 19 milli-loss at 6B and 30.1B. Pion reports a 35-milli-loss advantage over bfloat16 AdamW for a 1.3B model trained on 54B C4 tokens at context length 256, while keeping its own Lie-algebra momentum in fp32. At context length 4096, with the paper’s update settings and a Pion learning-rate sweep, Pion trails bfloat16 AdamW by 15.0 milli-loss and fp32 AdamW by 95.4 (Appendix W ). In both cases, storing the baseline in bfloat16 costs AdamW more than the reported advantage of the orthogonal method.

sections.heading: Different Layers, Different Manifolds: constraint versus optimizer.
sections.text: Yoshihara (2026) reports that assigning Stiefel constraints to attention and DGram constraints to MLP matrices lowers GPT-2 validation loss from 3.3855 without constraints and 3.3679 under all-Stiefel training to 3.3544; their Stiefel arm follows the manifold-Muon construction of Bernstein (2025) , and the result combines a module assignment with a projected-gradient optimizer. Our comparison is not a reproduction of that setting: it uses 360M models, blockwise d = 32 d=32 DGram instead of whole-matrix constraints, and our training recipe. Our controlled comparison fixes a blockwise d = 32 d=32 DGram geometry and varies its optimizer realization. Projected DGram keeps W ​ W ⊤ WW^{\top} diagonal, whereas W = diag ⁡ ( a ) ​ Q W=\operatorname{diag}(a)Q targets the same row geometry but assigns momentum, adaptive scaling, and regularization to different variables. Independent LR–WD tuning lowers projected DGram from 2.544 to 2.481; it remains behind tuned Muon (2.475) and d = 1 d=1 (2.462), and behind the per-row d = 32 d=32 reparameterization of the matched ladder (2.467). To test the module assignment, we keep one module type under d = 1 d=1 and replace the other (Appendix P ). Relative to training every matrix with d = 1 d=1 , DGram raises loss by 12.6 milli-loss in MLP matrices and 10.3 in attention matrices, and per-row d = 32 d=32 raises it by 2.6 and 3.2. Neither constraint improves on d = 1 d=1 in the module to which Yoshihara (2026) assign it, and the d = 32 d=32 penalty arises in both module types.

sections.heading: StelLA: norm control.
sections.text: StelLA constrains both low-rank factors in Equation 8 to Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2025 ) . In Llama-3-8B commonsense adaptation ( Llama Team, 2024 ) , we insert a product-of-spheres control between Euclidean and Stiefel factors. All runs use StelLA’s default S 0 = I S_{0}=I . Sphere improves over Euclidean by 2.12 accuracy points, whereas Stiefel changes Sphere by − 0.09 -0.09 points (Figure 2 ). All arms use StelLA’s default learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} . In a check over { 10 − 4 , 5 × 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 } \{10^{-4},5\times 10^{-4},10^{-3}\} , this is the best tested value for Sphere and Stiefel, while the best tested Euclidean rate, 10 − 3 10^{-3} , lies at the grid edge and remains 1.87 points below Sphere (Appendix X ). The Sphere gain is large, while adding row orthogonality does not improve accuracy. Factor-wise decay (U/V weight decay 1.0, the largest tested value) comes within 0.25 points of Sphere and recovers about 88% of the Euclidean-to-Sphere gain. In an update-rule ablation, a direct-polar Stiefel update improves over the canonical update by about 0.13 points (Appendix X ).

sections.heading: PSOFT: orthogonality within principal-subspace adaptation.
sections.text: PSOFT learns an orthogonal transformation restricted to a principal subspace of the pretrained weight ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Our controlled reconstruction holds fixed the selected subspace, rank, target modules, effective initialization, learned magnitude vectors, and training protocol. It compares PSOFT’s implemented Cayley/Neumann latent transformation with a dense latent transformation whose rows are optimized independently on spheres. Because the coordinate system and optimizer realization also change, this comparison tests the implemented orthogonal parameterization as a whole. At learning rates selected by validation loss, the row-sphere transform reaches 81.07 average accuracy, compared with 80.55 for PSOFT’s implementation and 80.95 for an unconstrained dense transform (Appendix Y ). Removing orthogonality between rows does not reduce accuracy, and the sphere constraint adds about 0.1 points over the dense transform at the selected rates and none at 8 × 10 − 4 8\times 10^{-4} . The ordering of PSOFT and row-sphere depends on the learning rate: PSOFT leads by 0.19 points at 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} and trails by 0.64 at 8 × 10 − 4 8\times 10^{-4} . The implemented five-term Neumann transform is also not exactly orthogonal; its singular values range from 0.86 to 1.00.

sections.heading: Stronger block constraints and row-mixing freedom.
sections.text: A monotone conditioning or diversity account predicts that decorrelating more row pairs should help, or at least not hurt. Instead, d = 8 d=8 has no resolved effect, d = 32 d=32 is worse in mean loss at all three 360M budgets, and, at 360M, matrix gains that restore within-block degrees of freedom, including row mixing, close the 6.5 milli-loss penalty of one scalar gain per block (Section 4.3 ). In trained 360M checkpoints, per-row d = 32 d=32 gives 32-row blocks a higher median stable rank than d = 1 d=1 (25.3 versus 21.6) and a lower median condition number (1.30 versus 1.54), yet it has higher loss (Appendix N ).

sections.heading: Optimizer realization matters alongside the constraint.
sections.text: The d = 1 d=1 gain agrees with recent norm-and-scale methods ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ; Hägele et al., 2026 ) , yet forward-normalized Muon, with the same function class, captures less than half of it (Section 4.5 ). Projected DGram and manifold Muon likewise show that a nominal constraint does not determine finite-budget performance independently of its optimizer. Norm and magnitude variables should be evaluated together with the state space in which momentum and preconditioning act.

sections.heading: Orthogonality claims are object-specific.
sections.text: Muon orthogonalizes an update, POET applies orthogonal transformations of a fixed random base matrix, OrthMuon constrains a directional factor whose effective rows remain orthogonal only under diagonal gains, and StelLA constrains the bases of a low-rank update. These interventions have different invariances, function classes, and induced optimizers, so evidence for one does not transfer to another; Muon’s success, for example, does not predict that orthogonal weights train better. We therefore suggest nested controls: an unconstrained baseline for the full recipe, a norm-matched sphere control for pairwise angles, matched gain granularity, an expressive matrix-gain control, and optimizer-specific tuning. The target metric and numerical policy should also be explicit: POET shows that an early-training advantage need not survive a completed schedule, and POET and Pion show that a full-bfloat16 AdamW baseline can trail the same baseline in fp32 by more than the reported gain. In both the pretraining ladder and the StelLA comparison, the comparison against the unconstrained baseline is positive, while the increment from row orthogonality is small or negative.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Appendix Z discusses the scope of our experiments.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We tested the incremental value of row orthogonality while holding per-row norm treatment and gain granularity fixed. In the matched diagonal-gain ladder, d = 8 d=8 has no resolvable effect relative to sphere optimization, and d = 32 d=32 worsens mean validation loss at 360M; the per-row gap is smaller at 1.3B and 3.1B and grows with block size. StelLA shows the same attribution in adaptation: sphere optimization supplies the gain over Euclidean factors, while adding Stiefel geometry provides no gain. Matrix-valued gains recover much of the large-block penalty but, used throughout the network, do not beat d = 1 d=1 . SPD factors on query and key projections give a small gain at 360M that shrinks with training length and fades as models grow. Manifold Muon trails d = 1 d=1 at every block size, budget, and scale. Beyond this small-model exception, no d > 1 d>1 realization provides a consistent advantage. Orthogonal updates, latent factors, and effective weights are distinct interventions. Attributing their benefits to orthogonality calls for sphere controls with matched magnitude freedom. In our settings, the direct evidence favors sphere optimization over hard block orthogonality.

sections.heading: Orthogonality in neural-network training.
sections.text: Orthogonal constraints have long been used to control signal propagation, conditioning, and robustness. Parseval Networks maintain linear operators as approximate tight frames, while Orthogonal Weight Normalization enforces rectangular weight orthogonality through a differentiable reparameterization ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) . Softer approaches penalize deviations from orthogonality ( Bansal et al., 2018 ) , whereas Cayley-transform methods optimize parameters directly on Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2020 ) . These objectives differ from spectral normalization, which controls the largest singular value without requiring weight vectors to be orthogonal to each other ( Miyato et al., 2018 ) . We revisit explicit weight orthogonality in Transformer training while separating it from per-vector norm control. Classical treatments develop optimization algorithms for Stiefel and related matrix manifolds ( Edelman et al., 1998 ; Absil et al., 2008 ) . In recurrent networks, soft orthogonality constraints outperformed exact constraints in the study of Vorontsov et al. (2017) ; our experiments compare hard block constraints with a norm-matched sphere control; soft orthogonality penalties are not evaluated here.

sections.heading: Geometry in parameter-efficient adaptation.
sections.text: Orthogonality enters parameter-efficient adaptation through several distinct constructions. OFT learns an orthogonal transformation of frozen pretrained weights; BOFT represents this transformation with butterfly factors; and PSOFT restricts it to a principal subspace ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . These methods apply orthogonality to transformations of pretrained geometry rather than directly to effective weight rows. Within low-rank adaptation, AdaLoRA uses softly orthogonal SVD-like factors for rank allocation, and OLoRA uses an orthonormal initialization without maintaining the constraint ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Büyükakyüz, 2024 ) . Recent methods optimize one or both LoRA factors on Stiefel manifolds ( Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , while RiemannLoRA optimizes the adapter on the fixed-rank matrix manifold to remove factorization ambiguity ( Bogachev et al., 2025 ) . Manifold-LoRA compares Stiefel and product-of-spheres constraints on a single LoRA basis ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our adaptation study makes this comparison within StelLA’s two-factor U ​ S ​ V ⊤ USV^{\top} parameterization and separates norm control from update design.

sections.heading: Geometry-aware language-model pretraining.
sections.text: Muon orthogonalizes matrix-valued updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2026b ) . Manifold Muon solves tangent-space spectral-norm steepest descent using fixed-point, dual-ascent, or exact closed-form solvers ( Su, 2025 ; Bernstein, 2025 ; Solonko et al., 2026 ) . It asks how to optimize a Stiefel-constrained weight; we ask whether that constraint improves over a sphere-constrained control with matched gain semantics. Hyperball fixes matrix Frobenius norms, while spectral-sphere optimization controls operator norms ( Wen et al., 2026a ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . Mano instead constructs tangent momentum from normalized weights and alternates row- and column-wise normalization of the update while keeping the weights in Euclidean space ( Gu and Xie, 2026 ) . POET learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random base matrix and preserves its initialized singular-value spectrum; Pion turns this isospectral structure into a direct optimizer based on left and right orthogonal transformations ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . Neither method requires orthogonal effective-weight rows. Module-wise Stiefel and DGram constraints have also been studied in Transformer pretraining ( Yoshihara, 2026 ) . An et al. (2026) compare Frobenius and spectral spheres with input- and output-oblique constraints, including their interactions with RMSNorm and weight decay. Our study holds per-row magnitude freedom fixed while directly testing the addition of orthogonality between rows.

sections.heading: Normalization and magnitude–direction separation.
sections.text: Weight normalization separates a vector into a normalized direction and a learned magnitude ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) . Muown is the closest prior parameterization and optimizer family to our d = 1 d=1 control, combining row-norm control with separately optimized magnitudes; AngularMuown relates this family to normalized directional updates ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ) . Other recent work combines fixed-norm directions with row or column gains, while Learnable Multipliers studies the benefit of freeing scalar, row, and column scales without normalizing directions ( Hägele et al., 2026 ; Velikanov et al., 2026 ) . Related language-model methods normalize broader collections of parameters or representations, including nGPT ( Loshchilov et al., 2025 ) , while DoRA applies magnitude–direction decomposition to low-rank adaptation ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation (NoRA) normalizes LoRA’s down-projection and also studies normalization at initialization only ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . Our d = 1 d=1 control confirms this norm-and-scale line of work; the new comparison begins when d d increases while per-row gains remain fixed.

sections.text: The constrained matrices are the q , k , v , o q,k,v,o projections and the MLP gate, up, and down projections. Embeddings, embedding-tied output parameters, and normalization weights remain in AdamW. Matrix rows are output channels, except that the MLP down projection is stored as an MLP-width-by-model-width matrix ( 3072 × 1024 3072\times 1024 at 360M) whose rows are its input channels; constraining its output-side rows instead gives the same loss. sections.heading: Manifold Muon.
sections.text: Manifold Muon solves spectral-norm steepest descent directly inside the Stiefel tangent space ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ; Solonko et al., 2026 ) , with the same magnitude parameterization and retraction as OrthMuon; Appendix C gives the full-width and thin-QR solvers.

sections.heading: Forward normalization.
sections.text: The same effective function class need not induce the same update. For w = a ​ q w=aq , the gain couples a step in q q to the effective angular step (Appendix C ). Forward normalization stores momentum on an unconstrained latent weight, applies Muon to it, and differentiates through row normalization; it preserves the d = 1 d=1 function class but changes the optimization trajectory. The default OrthMuon stores momentum in ambient coordinates; tangent and transported-momentum variants serve as further controls (Appendix S ).

sections.heading: No-gain control.
sections.text: Setting D k = I d D_{k}=I_{d} removes learned magnitudes. At d = 1 d=1 , this fixes every row norm without constraining angles between rows. Dense Muon, no-gain d = 1 d=1 , and learned-gain d = 1 d=1 form our norm-and-magnitude ablation.

sections.heading: MuonH/Hyperball.
sections.text: MuonH constrains the Frobenius norm of each full matrix to its initial value, explicitly normalizes its update, and uses no learned gain or weight decay ( Wen et al., 2026a ) . It is a coarser norm-control baseline with no pairwise orthogonality.

sections.heading: Appendix E Adaptation Setup
sections.text: For a base weight W 0 ∈ ℝ p × q W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q} , StelLA writes the rank- r r update as ( Li et al., 2025 ) Δ ​ W = α r ​ U ​ S ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ p × r , S ∈ ℝ r × r , V ∈ ℝ q × r . \Delta W=\frac{\alpha}{r}USV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r},\ S\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},\ V\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}. (8) The rank directions are the columns of U U and V V . Euclidean factors are unconstrained. Sphere optimizes each rank direction independently on a unit sphere while allowing arbitrary pairwise angles. Stiefel additionally requires U ⊤ ​ U = V ⊤ ​ V = I r U^{\top}U=V^{\top}V=I_{r} . All three use the same learned S S , making Stiefel versus Sphere the direct comparison for adding pairwise angle constraints at fixed factor norms. The canonical Stiefel update tangent-projects both the ambient gradient and the post-Adam displacement before polar retraction; the direct-polar control omits only the post-Adam tangent projection. The adaptation study uses Llama-3-8B with rank 32, α = 64 \alpha=64 , and adapters on the query, key, value, up-projection, and down-projection matrices ( Llama Team, 2024 ) . We train for three epochs with global batch 16, learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , linear decay, and 500 warmup steps. All main-table arms use StelLA’s default learning rate 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} and S 0 = I S_{0}=I ; each run loads the checkpoint with the lowest token-level loss on a fixed 120-example validation split. The learning-rate and decay grids in Appendix X are sensitivity checks, not selection rules for the main table. Scores are equal-weight macro accuracy over BoolQ, PIQA, SocialIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA.

sections.heading: Bounds on improvement.
sections.text: Because our claim is the absence of a gain, the relevant quantity is the largest improvement over d = 1 d=1 that each 95% interval still allows. Per-row d = 8 d=8 cannot improve on d = 1 d=1 by more than 4.9, 2.3, and 0.3 milli-loss at 2 × 2\times , 4 × 4\times , and 7.69 × 7.69\times ; per-row d = 32 d=32 is worse at every budget, and no interval allows an improvement. SPD d = 32 d=32 cannot improve by more than 4.6 milli-loss at 360M, 2.3 at 1.3B (1.1 against the gain-tuned d = 1 d=1 ), and 2.5 at 3.1B. Over the main ladder we make six d > 1 d>1 contrasts (two block sizes at three budgets) and do not adjust for multiplicity; after a Bonferroni correction for these six contrasts, d = 32 d=32 remains worse at 4 × 4\times and 7.69 × 7.69\times .

sections.heading: Appendix L Alternate-Corpus Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate the final 360M C4-trained checkpoints at 2 × 2\times and 7.69 × 7.69\times on six alternate-corpus sets without further training, at sequence length 4096, using 12.6M tokens per FPO set and 14.7M tokens per OLM set. Every checkpoint was also replayed on C4; the maximum deviation from its recorded loss was at most 0.0018 at both budgets. C4 removed every page containing a curly bracket ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) , which biases it away from code- and LaTeX-heavy pages. We therefore report the predominantly natural-language sets (FPO mixture, DCLM, OLM-Wiki) separately from StarCoder, ProofPile, and OLM-arXiv. Every arm has three seeds (Tables 22 and 23 ), and losses off C4 vary much more across seeds than on C4 (Table 25 ): the three d = 1 d=1 seeds span 1.5 milli-loss on C4 but 7–9 on the FPO mixture and DCLM and 59–106 on StarCoder, ProofPile, and OLM-arXiv. We therefore compare arms by seed-paired differences from d = 1 d=1 (Table 24 ). On the FPO mixture and DCLM, the C4 ordering carries over at about its C4 magnitude: per-row d = 8 d=8 and d = 32 d=32 are within noise of d = 1 d=1 , Muon and MuonH trail it by 7 to 14 milli-loss, and AdamW by about 90; across arms, these differences correlate with the C4 differences at r = 0.70 r=0.70 to 0.85 (AdamW excluded). OLM-Wiki is intermediate. On StarCoder, ProofPile, and OLM-arXiv, most paired intervals are wider than ± 80 \pm 80 milli-loss, and three seeds do not rank the arms; at 2 × 2\times , Muon is nominally better than d = 1 d=1 on ProofPile ( − 87 ± 83 -87\pm 83 ), a possible trade-off that these data do not establish. sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: The model is SiT-B/2, the DiT-B/2 architecture with width 768, 12 layers, and 12 heads of dimension 64; it has 130.5M parameters, of which 130.3M are trainable. The query, key, value, output, and MLP matrices (84.9M parameters, 65% of the total) receive the orthogonal parameterization; the adaLN modulation (42.5M), the embedders, and the final layer stay on AdamW in every arm. Training uses ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 , pre-encoded once with the SD-VAE ft-EMA autoencoder; each step draws a horizontal flip and a fresh posterior sample, which matches on-the-fly encoding in distribution. The global batch is 256 images (65,536 tokens per step). Training runs 500K steps with 1% linear warmup, a constant learning rate to 400K, and linear decay to zero over the last 100K steps, under bf16 autocast with fp32 weights, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, and an EMA decay of 0.9999. Weight decay is decoupled and is not applied to 1-D parameters or the class-embedding table. Query–key normalization applies a per-head RMSNorm to queries and keys, with learnable scales at the main learning rate and no decay. The Adam family uses β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) ; the Muon family uses momentum 0.95, Nesterov, and five Newton–Schulz steps. OrthAdam is the OrthMuon parameterization (unit-row directions with per-row gains) with an Adam update. Stiefel factors and gains receive no decay. Validation loss is measured on EMA weights over 10K validation images at 16 fixed time values with fixed noise. FID-50K comes from the official ADM evaluator with the SDE sampler (250 steps), no guidance, and sampling seed 0; sFID, IS, precision, and recall come from the same evaluator. sections.text: The matched ladder covers 360M models at four budgets and reports C4 validation loss. Kai Hu kaihu@cmu.edu Affiliation: Li Zhang Affiliation: Weichen Yu Affiliation: Matt Fredrikson Affiliation: Haoqi Hu Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Abstract A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every d d rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size d d is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no d > 1 d>1 used throughout the network reliably outperforms d = 1 d=1 , and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 , the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose. † † shortheadings: Orthogonality Beyond Sphere Optimization / Hu, Zhang, Yu, Fredrikson, and Hu † † firstpage: 1 keywords orthogonality constraints, Stiefel manifold, sphere optimization, Muon, language-model pre-training 1 Introduction Before the rise of large language models (LLMs), weight orthogonality was used to keep networks with millions of parameters well conditioned and their feature directions nonredundant ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) . For modern pretrained models, orthogonal fine-tuning methods report gains from learning orthogonal transformations of pretrained weights ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) or from constraining low-rank adapter factors to Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2025 ) . In LLM pre-training, orthogonality has so far mostly shaped the training dynamics rather than the weights: the Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the update to each weight matrix, and POET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random weight matrix, preserving its singular values. Research blogs ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) derive optimizers that keep the weights themselves on the Stiefel manifold, without large-scale language-model experiments. Yoshihara (2026) evaluates this approach in GPT-2 models with up to 124M parameters and assigns different orthogonality structures to attention and MLP matrices. Whether keeping the weights themselves orthogonal helps LLM pre-training at scale remains open. We study this question systematically with decoder-only models from 360M to 3.1B parameters trained on nearly 200B tokens. The most direct form of orthogonality training requires an entire weight matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m ≤ n m\leq n to have orthonormal rows, W ​ W ⊤ = I m WW^{\top}=I_{m} . This is a very strong regularization. It imposes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 constraints in total, so a square orthonormal matrix loses about half of its degrees of freedom, i.e., the number of effective parameters is roughly halved. We explored two routes for recovering the lost degrees of freedom. The first route relaxes the orthogonality constraint on W W to an orthogonal reparameterization of W W . The simplest variant adds per-row magnitudes: the model learns a row-orthonormal factor Q Q and a positive diagonal factor D D , and the effective weight is W = D ​ Q W=DQ . This reparameterization can represent every matrix whose rows are orthogonal and nonzero, but it recovers only m m degrees of freedom. Even with these magnitudes, full-matrix orthogonality substantially worsens validation loss, whether it is enforced by our projected update or by manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ) (Figure 1 ; Appendix M ). To go one step further, recall that every full-rank matrix admits a polar decomposition; we therefore replace the diagonal factor D D with a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix S S , so that W = S ​ Q W=SQ . This reparameterization recovers all m ​ n mn degrees of freedom: S S contributes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 and Q Q contributes m ​ n − m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 mn-m(m+1)/2 . A triangular factor ( W = T ​ Q W=TQ ) and a singular-value form ( W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} ) are equally expressive, but in training they recover much less of the constraint penalty than SPD, and the singular-value form recovers almost none. The second route relaxes the constraint itself. An n × n n\times n square matrix is partitioned into n / d n/d blocks of size d × n d\times n , and only each block is required to have orthonormal rows, so the number of constraints falls to n ⁡ ( d + 1 ) / 2 n(d+1)/2 . The block size d d becomes a single knob that ranges from d = 1 d=1 , which constrains only the row norms, to the shorter side of the matrix. Increasing d d adds exactly one thing: zero inner products between rows in the same block. The two routes combine: each block is reparameterized with per-row magnitudes, W k = D k ​ Q k W_{k}=D_{k}Q_{k} , or with an SPD factor, W k = S k ​ Q k W_{k}=S_{k}Q_{k} . Our main comparison uses per-row magnitudes at every block size, so increasing d d changes only the orthogonality between rows. In the special case d = 1 d=1 , the SPD factor reduces to the per-row magnitude, and the constraint reduces to a sphere constraint on each row with a learnable magnitude. Combining several ways to train orthonormal matrices with several ways to recover the lost degrees of freedom, we test fourteen variants, together with three alternative updates for the sphere control (Table 10 ), in pre-training Llama-style LLMs of three sizes, 360M, 1.3B, and 3.1B parameters, with token budgets from 2 × 2\times to 16 × 16\times the Chinchilla-optimal budget. No block size d > 1 d>1 used throughout the network reliably improves on d = 1 d=1 . Small blocks are indistinguishable from d = 1 d=1 , and the penalty grows steadily with block size. SPD factors, which restore mixing between rows of a block, recover much of this penalty at moderate block sizes but give no consistent advantage, and the other realizations trail d = 1 d=1 as well. The one placement that helps, SPD factors on the query and key projections, gives a small gain in our smallest model that fades as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 the orthogonality constraint reduces to sphere optimization: each row direction lives on its own unit sphere with a learned magnitude, and no relation between rows is imposed. We thus arrive, from the orthogonality side, at the direction–magnitude geometry of recent row-norm methods ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ; Hägele et al., 2026 ) , and like them we find that it improves on tuned Muon, as well as on MuonH, which fixes the Frobenius norm of each matrix ( Wen et al., 2026a ) , at every scale we trained. Across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows adds nothing beyond sphere optimization. However, the implementation of sphere optimization also matters: weight normalization ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) trained with Muon has the same expressiveness but recovers less than half of the improvement over Muon. This conclusion appears to conflict with several reports of orthogonality gains, so we re-examine five of them in pre-training and fine-tuning. The released implementations of POET and Pion store the AdamW baseline in bfloat16; with fp32 storage, AdamW improves by 80 to 150 milli-loss, POET’s short-run advantage shrinks from 31 to 9 milli-loss and reverses with longer training, and Pion trails AdamW by 95 milli-loss at 1.3B. For module-wise constraints, projected diagonal-Gram training trails a reparameterization that targets the same row geometry, and neither diagonal-Gram nor Stiefel blocks improve on d = 1 d=1 in the module to which they are assigned. In StelLA, replacing Euclidean adapter factors with sphere-constrained ones gains 2.1 accuracy points, and adding Stiefel constraints on top changes accuracy by − 0.09 -0.09 . In PSOFT, replacing the orthogonal latent transformation with independently normalized rows does not reduce accuracy. In each case, the reported gain traces to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to orthogonality between rows. Our contributions are: • A block-wise orthogonality family whose block size moves from sphere optimization to the largest Stiefel blocks each matrix allows while holding row magnitudes fixed, so that its effect isolates orthogonality between rows. • A pre-training study from 360M to 3.1B parameters showing that no block size above one used throughout the network improves on sphere optimization, that SPD factors on query and key projections give a small gain that vanishes as models grow, and that sphere optimization itself improves on tuned Muon; the same holds for a diffusion transformer on ImageNet, and fine-tuned models show no downstream advantage for any block size. • Re-examinations of five orthogonality methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that trace each reported gain to a factor other than orthogonality between rows. 2 Related Work Orthogonality in neural-network training. Orthogonal weights have been pursued through tight-frame, reparameterization, penalty, and manifold methods ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ; Bansal et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020 ) , distinct from spectral normalization ( Miyato et al., 2018 ) ; classical treatments develop the underlying matrix-manifold algorithms ( Edelman et al., 1998 ; Absil et al., 2008 ) . In the RNN study of Vorontsov et al. (2017) , soft orthogonality outperformed exact constraints. We compare hard block constraints with a norm-matched sphere control; soft orthogonality penalties are not evaluated here. Geometry in parameter-efficient adaptation. Orthogonality can constrain transformations of pretrained weights, SVD-like or initialized LoRA factors, or manifold-optimized adapters ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Büyükakyüz, 2024 ; Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Bogachev et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These constructions act on different objects. Our adaptation study compares sphere and Stiefel constraints within StelLA’s two-factor U ​ S ​ V ⊤ USV^{\top} parameterization. Geometry-aware language-model pretraining. Muon orthogonalizes matrix-valued updates, while manifold Muon asks how to optimize a Stiefel-constrained weight ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2026b ; Su, 2025 ; Bernstein, 2025 ; Solonko et al., 2026 ) ; we ask whether that constraint improves over a sphere control with matched gains. Related methods control Frobenius or operator norms, normalize update directions, or impose module-wise Stiefel and DGram geometry ( Wen et al., 2026a ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Gu and Xie, 2026 ; Yoshihara, 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . POET and Pion use orthogonal transformations but do not require orthogonal effective-weight rows ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . Normalization and magnitude–direction separation. Weight normalization separates direction from magnitude ( Salimans and Kingma, 2016 ) . Muown is the closest prior parameterization to our d = 1 d=1 control ( Lion et al., 2026 ; Hübler et al., 2026 ) ; related work studies row or column gains, broader parameter normalization, and magnitude–direction decompositions in adaptation ( Hägele et al., 2026 ; Velikanov et al., 2026 ; Loshchilov et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . Our d = 1 d=1 control confirms this norm-and-scale line; the new comparison begins when d d increases while per-row gains remain fixed. Concurrent work traces the gains of fixed-norm training largely to its effective learning rate ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . With the FPO-mix training mixture—92.57% DCLM, 6.09% StarCoder, and 1.34% ProofPile ( Wen et al., 2026b ) —and C4-val evaluation, d = 1 d=1 again leads MuonH and Muon at 360M and 1.3B, and per-row-gain d = 32 d=32 at 360M (Table 1 ; Appendix K ). On held-out web text, C4-trained 360M checkpoints keep the C4 ordering at about its C4 magnitude: on the FPO mixture and DCLM, per-row d = 8 d=8 and d = 32 d=32 match d = 1 d=1 , Muon and MuonH trail it by 7 to 14 milli-loss, and AdamW by about 90. On StarCoder, ProofPile, and OLM-arXiv, loss varies by 60–100 milli-loss between training runs of the same configuration, and no ordering among block sizes or baselines emerges (Appendix L ). The strength of the d = 1 d=1 control also extends beyond 360M. At 1.3B, it improves over Muon by 12.8, 13.1, and 12.0 milli-loss at 2 × 2\times , 4 × 4\times , and 7.77 × 7.77\times , and by 12.0 at 3.1B; Appendix J reports the full scaling table. The per-row d = 32 d=32 penalty shrinks with scale (Table 2 ), as does the query–key SPD gain, so both effects of row structure approach zero in the tested range; at 360M the d = 32 d=32 penalty corresponds to about 5% more training steps at every budget up to 16 × 16\times (Appendix H ). Sphere optimization also improves image generation. In a 130M-parameter diffusion transformer (SiT-B/2) trained on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 with query–key normalization, d = 1 d=1 lowers FID-50K from 25.50 to 24.60 with an Adam inner optimizer and from 21.55 to 20.81 with Muon, and lowers validation loss in both families. Query and key blocks of 64 rows do not improve on d = 1 d=1 , and an SPD factor on those blocks ties it (Appendix T ). Without query–key normalization, AdamW and d = 1 d=1 occasionally diverge late in training, whereas scalar-gain d > 1 d>1 blocks, which bound the query–key product, never do. Query–key normalization removes these divergences and gives lower FID than d > 1 d>1 without it, so the stability benefit of d > 1 d>1 traces to logit control rather than to orthogonality between rows. Fine-tuning does not separate the parameterizations either. After full fine-tuning of the 3.1B models on Commonsense170K, with the merged weights trained by one AdamW recipe, eight-task accuracy differs from the matched d = 1 d=1 model by at most 0.4 points for every d > 1 d>1 and query–key configuration, well within the variation between fine-tuning runs. Muon and MuonH trail d = 1 d=1 by 0.7 and 1.1 points.
